Background: About Economic Survey


   •    It is an annual flagship document released by the government (specifically the Ministry of Finance)
       that reviews the state of the economy over the past financial year.
   •    It analyzes macroeconomic and sectoral performance, highlights policy initiatives, and provides a
      growth outlook for the upcoming year.
   •  Prepared By: The Economic Division of the Department of Economic Affairs, under the supervision
       of the Chief Economic Adviser (CEA).
   •   Historical Context: It was first introduced in 1950–51, and since 1964, it has been published as an
      independent document separate from the Budget.
   •  Key Components Analyzed: The survey evaluates the country's financial health across several core
       metrics:
       §  Macroeconomic Data: Outlines Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth projections, inflation
            rates, and fiscal deficit figures.
       §  Sectoral Performance: Evaluates progress and constraints in agriculture, industrial
          manufacturing, infrastructure, and the services sector.
       §  External Sector: Details performance metrics regarding foreign direct investments (FDI), import-
          export volumes, and foreign exchange reserves.
       §   Social Infrastructure: Assesses employment numbers, healthcare, education, and rural
         development milestones.
   •  Importance:
       §  The "Report Card": It serves as a comprehensive, data-driven report on India's economic
           health, detailing metrics like GDP growth, inflation, employment, and fiscal developments.
       §  Precursor to the Budget: Tabled in Parliament one day ahead of the Union Budget, it lays out
          the economic context and policy recommendations needed for informed budgetary resource
            allocation.
       §  Forward-Looking: It pinpoints key economic concerns and maps out strategic directions to
          ensure sustainable growth in the short and medium term.
   •  Economic Survey vs. Union Budget
       §  Economic Survey is backward-looking and diagnostic. It highlights what happened in the
        economy during the last 12 months and makes growth projections.
       §  Union Budget is forward-looking and policy-oriented. It functions as an official statement
           detailing government expenditure, tax allocations, and revenue generation plans for the
         upcoming fiscal year.

   Highlights of Economic Survey 2025-26


State of the Economy

   •  Global Context: The global environment remains fragile with growth holding up better than
      expected but risks elevated amid intensifying geopolitical tensions, trade fragmentation, and
        financial vulnerabilities. The impact of these shocks may still surface with a lag.
   •   India's GDP Performance: India's First Advance Estimates place FY26 real GDP growth at 7.4% and
     GVA growth at 7.3% — reaffirming India's status as the fastest-growing major economy for the
       fourth consecutive year.





   •  Consumption: Private Final Consumption Expenditure (PFCE) grew by 7.0% in FY26, reaching 61.5%
       of GDP — the highest since 2012 (FY23 also recorded 61.5%).
      §  Growth supported by: low inflation, stable employment, increasing real purchasing power
      §  Strong agricultural performance boosting rural consumption
      §  Improvements in urban consumption aided by tax rationalisation, indicate broad-based
        demand momentum.
   •  Investment: Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) grew by 7.8% in FY26, with its share remaining
       steady at 30% of GDP, supported by sustained public capital expenditure and revival in private
       investment as evident from corporate announcements.
   •  Supply Side — Services: Services remain the main driver of growth. GVA for services grew by 9.3%
        in H1 FY26, with estimated 9.1% growth for the full fiscal year — indicating broad-based sectoral
       expansion.





                                                                                                                         pg. 3

[Type here]



                                         Quick Revision Facts

             •  FY26 Real GDP Growth: 7.4% | GVA Growth: 7.3%
             •   India: Fastest-growing major economy — 4th consecutive year
             •  PFCE growth: 7.0% | Share in GDP: 61.5% — highest since 2012
             •  GFCF growth: 7.8% | Share in GDP: 30%
             •   Services GVA growth (H1 FY26): 9.3% | Full year estimate: 9.1%
             •  Key consumption drivers: Low inflation, stable employment, tax rationalisation & strong
                  agriculture


Fiscal Developments: Anchoring Stability through Credible
Consolidation

   •  Sovereign Credit Upgrades: Government’s prudent fiscal management has strengthened credibility
      and reinforced confidence in India’s macroeconomic and fiscal framework. This led to three
       sovereign credit rating upgrades in 2025 - by
      §  Morningstar DBRS
      §  S&P Global Ratings
      §  Rating and Investment Information (R&I), Inc
   •  Revenue Receipts: Centre's revenue receipts strengthened from an average of about 8.5% of GDP
       (FY16–FY20) to 9.2% of GDP in FY25 (PA).
       §   This improvement was driven by buoyant non-corporate tax collections, which rose from about
         2.4% of GDP pre-pandemic to about 3.3% post-pandemic.
   •  Direct Tax Base Expansion: Income tax returns filed increased from 6.9 crore (FY22) to 9.2 crore
       (FY25).
       §  Higher return filing reflects improved compliance, greater technology use in tax administration,
         and a growing number of individuals entering the tax net as their income rise.
   •  GST Collections: Gross GST collections (April–December 2025): ₹17.4 lakh crore, registering year-on
       year (YoY) growth of 6.7%
       §  GST revenue growth is broadly aligned with prevailing nominal GDP growth conditions.
       §   In parallel, high-frequency indicators suggest robust transaction volumes, with cumulative e-
        way bill volumes (April–December 2025) growing by 21% YoY.
   •   Capital Expenditure: Effective Capex of Central Government rose from average 2.7% of GDP (pre-
      pandemic) to about 3.9% post-pandemic and to a higher 4% of GDP in FY25
   •  SASCI (Special Assistance to States for Capital Expenditure): Through it, Centre has incentivised
       States to maintain capital spending at around 2.4% of GDP in FY25
   •  State Finances & Debt: Combined fiscal deficit of State Governments stayed broadly stable at
      around 2.8% of GDP in the post-pandemic period (similar to pre-pandemic levels), but has edged up
        in recent years to 3.2% in FY25, reflecting emerging pressures on State finances.
   •  General government debt-to-GDP ratio: Reduced by about 7.1 percentage points since 2020, even
       while maintaining high public investment.
                                         Quick Revision Facts

             •  3 credit rating upgrades (2025): Morningstar DBRS, S&P Global Ratings & R&I Inc.
             •  Revenue receipts: 8.5% GDP (FY16-20) → 9.2% GDP (FY25)
             •   Non-corporate tax: 2.4% GDP (pre-pandemic) → 3.3% GDP (post-pandemic)
             •   ITR filings: 6.9 crore (FY22) → 9.2 crore (FY25)

             •  GST collections (Apr–Dec 2025): ₹17.4 lakh crore | Growth: 6.7%
             •  E-way bill volume growth: 21% y-o-y (Apr–Dec 2025)
             •   Central Capex: 2.7% GDP (pre-pandemic) → 3.9% (post-pandemic) → 4% (FY25)
             •   State Capex (via SASCI): ~2.4% of GDP (FY25)
             •   State fiscal deficit: ~2.8% GDP (post-pandemic) → 3.2% in FY25
             •  Govt debt-to-GDP reduction since 2020: ~7.1 percentage points


Monetary Management and Financial Intermediation:
Refining The Regulatory Touch

   •  Monetary aspects: India's monetary and financial sectors have exhibited robust performance in
      FY26 (April-December 2025), underpinned by strategic policy actions and structural resilience
       across financial intermediation channels.
   •  Banking Sector Performance: Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs) demonstrated significant
      improvement in asset quality as evidenced by their
       §  Gross NPA ratio: 2.2% (September 2025) — multi-decadal low
       §  Net NPA ratio: 0.5% (September 2025) — record low
       §  YoY credit growth of SCBs (as of December 2025): Increased to 14.5% (up from 11.2% in
         December 2024)
   •   Financial Inclusion
       §  Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) (launched in 2014): Helped in establishing
          foundational savings and transaction infrastructure for previously unbanked populations with
        o  Accounts opened: 55.02 crore (as of March 2025)
        o  Rural & semi-urban accounts: 36.63 crore
       §  Stand-Up India Scheme: Offers bank loans of ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore for SC, ST, and women
          entrepreneurs for establishing greenfield enterprises.
       § PM Street Vendor's Aatmanirbhar Nidhi (PM SVANidhi) scheme: Provides collateral-free
          working capital loans to street vendors.
       §  Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana (PMMY): It is financing micro and small enterprises in
          manufacturing, trading, services, and allied agricultural activities
        o  By October 2025, the scheme had disbursed over ₹36.18 lakh crore across 55.45 crore loan
              accounts.
   •   Capital Markets & Investor Participation
       §  Demat accounts added (FY26 till December 2025): 235 lakh of demat accounts were added,
          pushing the total count beyond 21.6 crore.
        o  Key milestone: Crossing of the 12-crore mark for unique investors in September 2025, with
               nearly a fourth of them being women.
       §  Mutual fund industry also expanded, with 5.9 crore unique investors (as of the end of
         December 2025), of which 3.5 crore (as of November 2025) were from non-tier-I and tier-II
             cities
        o  Reflects the diffusion of financial participation beyond traditional urban centres.
   •   India's first International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) at GIFT City — creating an enabling
      ecosystem to attract global capital
   •  International Validation — FSAP 2025: The systemic rise in regulatory quality has received
       international validation through the Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP) conducted jointly
      by IMF and World Bank in 2025.

                                                                                                                         pg. 5

[Type here]



       §  Both reports noted an increasingly resilient, diversified, and inclusive financial system, with
        o  Total financial sector assets at nearly 187% of GDP in CY 2024
        o  Capital markets expanding from 144% of GDP (in CY 2017) to 175% (in CY 2024).
       §  The assessments found that banks and NBFCs possess adequate capital buffers even under
          severe stress scenarios.
                                         Quick Revision Facts

            •  SCB Gross NPA: 2.2% (Sep 2025) — multi-decadal low | Net NPA: 0.5% — record low
            •  SCB credit growth: 14.5% (Dec 2025) vs 11.2% (Dec 2024)
            •  PMJDY accounts: 55.02 crore | Rural/semi-urban: 36.63 crore
            •  Stand-Up India: Loans ₹10 lakh–₹1 crore for SC/ST/Women entrepreneurs
            •  PMMY disbursement: ₹36.18 lakh crore across 55.45 crore accounts (Oct 2025)
            •  Demat accounts (total): 21.6 crore+ | Added in FY26: 235 lakh
            •  Unique investors: Crossed 12 crore (Sep 2025) | Women: ~25%
            •  MF unique investors: 5.9 crore | Non-Tier I & II cities: 3.5 crore
            •   GIFT City: India's first IFSC
            •  FSAP (IMF & World Bank, 2025): Financial sector assets = 187% of GDP | Capital markets
              = 175% of GDP (CY 2024)
            •   Capital markets grew from 144% (CY 2017) → 175% (CY 2024) of GDP


External Sector: Playing the Long Game

   •   India’s Global Trade Share
       §  Share in global merchandise exports nearly doubled from 1% (CY 2005) to 1.8% (CY 2024)
       §  Share in global commercial services exports more than doubled from 2% (CY 2005) to 4.3% (CY
          2024)
       §  As per UNCTAD's Trade and Development Report 2025, India ranked among the leading
         economies in trade partner diversification,
        o  Ranking 3rd in the Global South
        o  Recorded a trade diversity score higher than all Global North economies.
   •  Exports Performance (FY25)
       §  Total exports (FY25): Reached record US $825.3 billion, registering Y-o-Y growth of 6.1%,
          driven primarily by robust growth in services exports.
       §  Non-petroleum exports: Reached historic high of US $374.3 billion
       §  Non-petroleum, non-gems & jewellery exports: Constituted nearly four-fifths of aggregate
         merchandise exports
       §  Services exports: Touched all-time high of US $387.6 billion, growing by 13.6% — reinforcing
           India as a global hub for technology and business services
   •   India’s Current Account Deficit (CAD): Remained moderate, supported by strong net inflows from
       services exports and remittances that offset the merchandise trade deficit.
       §   In Q2 FY26, India’s CAD, at around 1.3% of GDP, compared favourably with several other major
          economies.
   •  Remittances (FY25): India remained the world’s largest recipient of remittances, with inflows
       reaching US $135.4 billion in FY25, supporting stability in the external account.
       §  Share of remittances from advanced economies increased, reflecting a growing contribution
         from skilled and professional workers.

                                                                                                                         pg. 6

[Type here]



   •  Foreign Exchange Reserves: Increased to US $701.4 billion (as of 16 January 2026)
       §  Providing import cover of about 11 months
       §  Covering over 94% of external debt, thereby strengthening resilience against external volatility.
   •  Foreign Direct Investment: Amid a subdued global investment environment, India continued to
        attract substantial foreign direct investment, with
       §  Gross FDI inflows reached USD 64.7 billion during April-November 2025.
       §   India ranked 4th globally in Greenfield investment announcements in 2024, with over 1,000
           projects
       §   India emerged as the largest destination for Greenfield digital investments between 2020-24.


                                         Quick Revision Facts

             •  Merchandise export share: 1% (CY 2005) → 1.8% (CY 2024)
             •  Commercial services export share: 2% (CY 2005) → 4.3% (CY 2024)
             •  UNCTAD Trade Diversity Rank: 3rd in Global South | Higher than all Global North
              economies
             •   Total exports FY25: USD 825.3 billion | Growth: 6.1%
             •   Services exports FY25: USD 387.6 billion | Growth: 13.6% — all-time high
             •  Non-petroleum exports FY25: USD 374.3 billion — historic high
             •  CAD (Q2 FY26): ~1.3% of GDP
             •   Remittances FY25: USD 135.4 billion — world's largest recipient
             •   Forex reserves (16 Jan 2026): USD 701.4 billion | Import cover: ~11 months | External
               debt coverage: 94%+
             •   Gross FDI (Apr–Nov 2025): USD 64.7 billion
             •   Greenfield investment rank (2024): 4th globally | 1,000+ projects
             •   Greenfield digital investment (2020-24): India = largest destination globally


Inflation: Tamed and Anchored

   •   Historic Low Inflation: India recorded its lowest-ever inflation rate since the beginning of the CPI
        series.
       §  Average headline inflation for April–December 2025 stood at just 1.7%, marking a significant
          milestone in India's macroeconomic management.
   •  Reason: Moderation in retail inflation was primarily driven by a disinflationary trend in food and
        fuel prices.
       §  These two categories together constitute 52.7% of India's Consumer Price Index (CPI) basket.
   •  Among major Emerging Markets & Developing Economies (EMDEs), India recorded one of the
       sharpest declines in headline inflation in 2025 compared to 2024
       §   Fall of approximately 1.8 percentage points
                                         Quick Revision Facts
            •  Average Headline Inflation (April–December 2025): 1.7%
            •  Food + Fuel weight in CPI basket: 52.7%
            •   Decline over 2024 (YoY) by ~1.8 percentage points
            •   India's global standing: Among sharpest declines in EMDEs
               §

Agriculture & Food Management

   •   Livestock: Livestock sector witnessed strong growth, with GVA rising by nearly 195% (between FY15
      and FY24)
   •   Fisheries: Fish production increased by more than 140% during 2014–2024, significantly outpacing
      growth recorded in the previous decade (2004–14)
   •  Foodgrain Production: India's foodgrain production estimated at 3,577.3 Lakh Metric Tonnes (LMT)
        in Agriculture Year (AY) 2024–25, an increase of 254.3 LMT over the previous year
       §  Boosted by a good monsoon season in 2024
       §  Growth driven by higher output of Rice, Wheat, Maize and Coarse Cereals (Shree Anna)
   •  Horticulture overtakes Foodgrain Production
       §   Horticulture accounts for about 33% of Agricultural GVA, has emerged as a key driver of
            agricultural growth.
       §   Horticulture production reached 362.08 Million Tonnes (MT) in 2024–25
       §  Surpassed estimated foodgrain production of 357.73 MT — a significant structural shift in
           Indian agriculture
   •   Agricultural Marketing & Infrastructure: To improve efficiency in agricultural marketing and
        infrastructure, the Government is implementing
       §  Agriculture Marketing Infrastructure (AMI) sub-scheme under ISAM
       §  Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) to strengthen farm-gate facilities and encourage private
           sector participation.
       §  e-NAM Scheme to enhance price discovery.
        o  As of 31 December 2025, it has onboarded about 1.79 crore farmers, 2.72 crore traders and
             4,698 FPOs, covering 1,522 mandis across 23 States and 4 UTs.
   •  Farmer Income Support & Social Protection: Farmers’ incomes are supported through assured MSP
        for mandated crops and PM-KISAN income transfers.
       §  PM Kisan Maandhan Yojana (PMKMY) provides pension support, strengthening farmers’ income
           security and social protection.
        o  Since its inception, more than ₹4.09 lakh crore has been released to eligible farmers in 21
              instalments
        o  Under PMKMY, 24.92 lakh farmers are enrolled as of 31 December 2025.

Services: From Stability to New Frontiers

   •   India's services sector share in GDP rose to 53.6% in H1 FY26.
   •   Services' share in GVA reached an all-time high of 56.4% as per the First Advance Estimate (FAE) of
       FY26, reflecting the rising weight of modern, tradable, and digitally delivered services.
   •   India in Global Services Trade: India is now the world's 7th-largest exporter of services.
       §   India's share in global services trade more than doubled from 2% in 2005 to 4.3% in 2024.
   •  Services as Top FDI Destination: The services sector remains the largest recipient of FDI in India,
       accounting for an average of 80.2% of total FDI during FY23–FY25, up from 77.7% during the pre-
      pandemic period (FY16–FY20).
                                         Quick Revision Facts
            •   Services share in GDP — 53.6% in H1 FY26
            •   Services share in GVA — 56.4% (all-time high, FAE FY26)
            •   India's rank in global services exports — 7th largest

                                                                                                                         pg. 8

[Type here]



            •   India's share in global services trade — 2% (2005) → 4.3% (2024)
            •   Services share in total FDI — 80.2% (FY23–FY25) vs 77.7% (FY16–FY20, pre-pandemic)


Industry's Next Leap: Structural Transformation & Global
Integration

   •   Industrial activity strengthened in FY26: Industry GVA growing 7.0% (real terms) in H1, despite
      subdued and persistent global headwinds.
   •  Manufacturing growth accelerated: GVA expanding 7.72% in Q1 and 9.13% in Q2 FY26, reflecting
        structural recovery.
   •  Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Schemes across 14 sectors have attracted over ₹2.0 lakh crore of
       actual investment, generating incremental production/sales exceeding ₹18.7 lakh crore and over
       12.6 lakh jobs as of September 2025.
   •   India’s innovation performance: Strengthened steadily, with its Global Innovation Index rank
       improving to 38th in 2025 from 66th in 2019.
   •   India Semiconductor Mission: It has advanced domestic capabilities, with 10 semiconductor
       manufacturing and packaging projects approved across 6 States, involving about ₹1.60 lakh crore of
       investment.
                                         Quick Revision Facts
            •   Industry GVA growth — 7.0% (H1 FY26, real terms)
            •  Manufacturing GVA — 7.72% (Q1) & 9.13% (Q2 FY26)
            •   PLI Schemes — 14 sectors, ₹2.0 lakh crore investment, ₹18.7 lakh crore production, 12.6
                 lakh jobs
            •   Global Innovation Index — 38th (2025) vs 66th (2019)
            •  Semiconductor projects approved — 10 projects, 6 States, ₹1.60 lakh crore investment


Investment and Infrastructure: Strengthening Connectivity,
Capacity and Competitiveness

   •   Capital Expenditure: Centre's capital expenditure increased nearly 4.2 times, from ₹2.63 lakh crore
        in FY18 to ₹11.21 lakh crore in FY26 (BE).
       §   Effective capital expenditure in FY26 stands at ₹15.48 lakh crore, positioning infrastructure as a
          key growth driver.
   •  Roads & Highways: National Highway network grew by about 60%, from 91,287 km in FY14 to
       1,46,572 km in FY26 (up to December).
       §  Operational High-Speed Corridors expanded nearly ten-fold, from 550 km (FY14) to 5,364 km
           (FY26).
   •  Railways: India's rail network reached 69,439 route km as of March 2025, with a targeted addition
       of 3,500 km in FY26.
       §  Railway electrification achieved 99.1% by October 2025.
   •  Aviation: India has emerged as the world's third-largest domestic aviation market. The number of
       operational airports increased from 74 in 2014 to 164 in 2025.
   •  Power Sector: Installed power capacity rose 11.6% (y-o-y) to 509.74 GW as of November 2025.
                                                                                                                         pg. 9

[Type here]



       §  Demand-supply gap declined from 4.2 per cent in FY14 to nil by November 2025.
       §  DISCOMs recorded a positive Profit After Tax (PAT) of ₹2,701 crore in FY25 for the first time.
       §  AT&C losses reduced from 22.62% (FY14) to 15.04% (FY25).
       §  Renewable energy constitutes 49.83% of total installed capacity, with India ranking third
           globally in overall RE and installed solar capacity.
   •  Telecom: Tele-density reached 86.76%, with 5G services available in 99.9% of districts across India.
   •   Jal Jeevan Mission: Over 81% of rural households have access to clean tap water under the Jal
      Jeevan Mission as of October 2025.
   •  Space: India became the fourth nation globally to achieve autonomous satellite docking through
       the SpaDeX mission, alongside expanded indigenous missions and growing private sector
        participation.
                                         Quick Revision Facts

             •  Capex growth — ₹2.63 lakh crore (FY18) → ₹11.21 lakh crore (FY26 BE), 4.2x rise
             •  NH network — 91,287 km (FY14) → 1,46,572 km (FY26)
             •  High-Speed Corridors — 550 km (FY14) → 5,364 km (FY26), ~10x rise
             •   Rail network — 69,439 route km, electrification at 99.1%
             •   Airports — 74 (2014) → 164 (2025); India = 3rd largest aviation market
             •   Installed power capacity — 509.74 GW; demand-supply gap = nil
             •  RE share in installed capacity — 49.83%; India = 3rd globally in RE & solar
             •  DISCOMs PAT — ₹2,701 crore (FY25), first-ever positive
             •  AT&C losses — 22.62% (FY14) → 15.04% (FY25)
             •  5G coverage — 99.9% of districts
             •   Jal Jeevan Mission — 81% rural households covered
             •  SpaDeX — India — 4th nation for autonomous satellite docking


Environment & Climate Change: Building a Resilient,
Competitive and Development-Driven India

   •  Renewable Energy Capacity Addition (2025-26): During 2025-26 (up to 31st December 2025), India
        installed a total of 38.61 GW of renewable energy capacity.
       §   Solar power led the addition with 30.16 GW, followed by hydro power at 3.24 GW, wind power
           at 4.47 GW, and bio-power at 0.03 GW.
                                         Quick Revision Facts

               •   Total RE capacity installed (2025-26, till Dec 2025) — 38.61 GW
               •   Solar — 30.16 GW
               •  Wind — 4.47 GW
               •  Hydro — 3.24 GW
               •   Bio-Power — 0.03 GW

Education & Health: What Works and What's Next

   •  School Education: India operates one of the world's largest school systems, serving 24.69 crore
       students across 14.71 lakh schools, supported by over 1.01 crore teachers (UDISE+ 2024-25).
       §  stands at 90.9 at primary stage (Grade I–V), 90.3 at upper primary (Grade VI–VIII), 78.7 at
          secondary stage (Grade IX–X), and 58.4 at higher secondary (Grade XI–XII).
       §  Key schemes driving enrolment and equity include Poshan Shakti Nirman and Samagra Shiksha
          Abhiyan.
   •  Higher Education: Number of Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) increased from 51,534 in 2014-15
       to 70,018 as of June 2025.
       §  Premier institutions have expanded significantly, with India now having 23 IITs, 21 IIMs, and 20
          AIIMS.
        o  Two international IIT campuses have been established in Zanzibar and Abu Dhabi.
       §  Under the National Education Policy (NEP), key reforms include the National Credit Framework
           (NCrF), adopted by 170 universities, blending academic and skills-based learning.
       §  Academic Bank of Credit covers 2,660 institutions with over 4.6 crore IDs issued, including 2.2
          crore APAAR IDs.
       §   Additionally, 153 universities have introduced flexible entry-exit pathways and biannual
          admissions, working towards the NEP target of 50% GER by 2035.
   •  Health: India has achieved remarkable progress in maternal and child health since 1990.
       §  Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR): Declined by 86%, far exceeding the global average reduction
           of 48%.
       §  Under-Five Mortality Rate (U5MR): Fell by 78%, surpassing the global reduction of 61%
       §  Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR): Dropped by 70% against a global decline of 54% during 1990–
          2023.
       §   Infant Mortality Rate (IMR): Declined by over 37% in the past decade, falling from 40 deaths
          per thousand live births in 2013 to 25 in 2023.
                                         Quick Revision Facts

             •   Total students — 24.69 crore across 14.71 lakh schools; teachers — 1.01 crore
             •  GER — Primary 90.9 | Upper Primary 90.3 | Secondary 78.7 | Higher Secondary
               58.4
             •   HEIs — 51,534 (2014-15) → 70,018 (June 2025)
             •  Premier institutions — 23 IITs, 21 IIMs, 20 AIIMS
             •   International IITs — Zanzibar & Abu Dhabi
             •  NCrF adopted by — 170 universities
             •  Academic Bank of Credit — 2,660 institutions, 4.6 crore IDs, 2.2 crore APAAR IDs
             •   Flexible pathways — 153 universities; NEP GER target — 50% by 2035
             • MMR decline — 86% (India) vs 48% (Global)
             •  U5MR decline — 78% (India) vs 61% (Global)
             •  NMR decline — 70% (India) vs 54% (Global)
             •  IMR — 40 (2013) → 25 (2023), over 37% decline

Employment & Skill Development: Getting Skilling Right

   •  Employment Overview: Total of 56.2 crore people (aged 15 years and above) were employed in Q2
       FY26, reflecting a creation of around 8.7 lakh new jobs in Q2 compared to Q1 FY26.
       §  Organised manufacturing sector recorded a 6% YoY increase in employment in FY24 (as per
         Annual Survey of Industries), translating to an addition of over 10 lakh jobs compared to FY23.
   •  Gig & Platform Workers: Labour Codes have formally recognised gig and platform workers,
       extending social security, welfare funds, and benefit portability to this growing workforce segment.
   •  e-Shram Portal: As of January 2026, the e-Shram portal has registered over 31 crore unorganised
       workers.
       §  Notably, women account for over 54% of total registrants, strengthening the reach of gender-
          focused welfare schemes.
   •  National Career Service (NCS) Portal: Serves as a one-stop solution connecting job seekers,
       employers, and training providers.
       §    It has over 5.9 crore registered job seekers, 53 lakh job providers, and has mobilised
          approximately 8 crore vacancies across diverse sectors.
   •   Skill Ecosystem — ITI Upgradation: National Scheme for Upgradation of ITIs proposes to upgrade
       1,000 government ITIs, comprising 200 Hub ITIs and 800 Spoke ITIs, through smart classrooms,
      modern labs, digital content, and industry-aligned courses.
                                     Quick Revision Facts

             •   Total employed (Q2 FY26) — 56.2 crore (15 years & above)
             •  New jobs created in Q2 vs Q1 FY26 — 8.7 lakh

From Import Substitution to Strategic Resilience and
Strategic Indispensability

   •   Disciplined Approach to 'Swadeshi': The Economic Survey emphasises that 'Swadeshi' must be a
       disciplined strategy, as not all import substitution is feasible or desirable.
       §  Three-tiered framework is proposed to guide indigenisation decisions, distinguishing between
             critical vulnerabilities with high strategic urgency, economically feasible capabilities with
           strategic payoffs, and areas of low strategic urgency or high-cost substitution.
   •  National Input Cost Reduction Strategy: National Input Cost Reduction Strategy is recommended,
       treating competitiveness as infrastructure — recognising that affordable and reliable inputs are
      fundamental to industrial strength and global competitiveness.
   •  From Swadeshi to Strategic Indispensability: The Survey outlines a clear progression — from
       'Swadeshi' to Strategic Resilience to Strategic Indispensability — where intelligent import
       substitution invests in national strength and ultimately embeds India deeply in global supply
       systems. The end goal is shifting the world from "thinking about buying Indian" to "buying Indian
       without thinking."
